newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions have upper hand in new wage talks.
newsitem.headline: German unions have upper hand in new wage talks.

text.p: German trade unions on Tuesday were seen entering wage negotiations for 1997 with the strongest cards firmly in their hands following a humiliating climb-down by the Gesamtmetall employers group on sick pay cuts.

IG Metall, the union which on Monday forced the metal and electronics employers federation to back down, goes into full wage negotiations later this week with the knowledge that communications in the opposition camp are at best strained.

German companies have been left bemused by Gesamtmetall's reversal of an earlier recommendation that they immediately implement new laws to cut sick pay, together with a similar reticence shown by employer federations in other industries.

"It is an act of enormous stupidity to react in this way to political decisions favourable to business," Eberhard Hamer, head of the Mittelstandsinstitut for the influential small corporate sector, wrote in a newspaper article on Tuesday.
The Federal government last month passed a controversial new law allowing companies to cut sick pay to 80 percent of the normal wage from 100 percent currently.
The legislation stirred protest from labour leaders, who argued that such benefits are enshrined in pay agreements and can thus only be removed in direct negotiation with the unions.
An ensuing wave of worker protest forced Gesamtmetall and many firms who had hurried to follow the advice and implement the new law, into an embarrassing backtrack on Monday.

Employers' groups in areas such as the retail sector have decided against full implementation of the new laws, despite not having faced the mass protests that hit the metalworking and engineering sector last week.

Hamer said that employer groups now ran the risk that "politicians would no longer take seriously their demands" to improve the German business location, such as the long-standing call by German business for lower labour costs.

Employer federation leaders such as Gesamtmetall chairman Werner Stumpfe are now in turn questioning how sincere the support of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government is for industry on the issue of labour costs.
"It is unprecedented in the history of this country that a government passes a law only to warn against it being put into effect," Stumpfe said after Monday's meeting with IG Metall.

Sensing disarray among the employers, the trade unions, which say their membership numbers have been rising steadily since the start of the sick pay dispute, are meanwhile seeking to turn the wider debate on labour costs to their advantage.

"The unions are aware of the need to reduce costs, but that shouldn't happen simply through unilateral measures such as sick pay cuts for the employees," Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the DGB trade union umbrella group said on radio.

Engelen-Kefer said that improvements in safety and other health measures at work could ultimately result in savings of up to 100 billion marks ($65.5 billion) from lower absenteeism -- compared to the 12 billion marks that the envisaged 20 percent sick pay cut would save.

A more likely immediate outcome of Monday's retreat by employers, however, is that IG Metall will be further enboldened not to make any concessions with 1997 wage claim recommendations, due to be made known later on Tuesday.
With up to 120,000 jobs in the industry being lost each year, firm employment protection guarantees will be one of the cornerstones of its demands.

But it will now be tempted to seek a wage deal as advantageous to metal and engineering workers as the last pact pact, which assured them two rises, one of 3.4 percent and a second of 3.6 percent, in the 1996 year. ($1=1.5252 Mark)
